title: "Null hypotheses and test statistics"
execute:
  enabled: true

A hypothesis test begins with a parameter claim and a statistic that standardizes the discrepancy between that claim and the data. The null value, estimator, and standard error must refer to the same unit and estimand.

The [standard-error page](standard-errors.qmd#deriving-the-standard-error-of-a-mean) showed how an estimator varies across samples. A test adds a reference claim: it asks how unusual the random statistic would be if that claim and its sampling assumptions generated the data.

Those sampling assumptions include the [independence](../foundations/independence.qmd) structure of the observation units. In the paired vowel analysis, the independent modeled units are speaker-level differences, not the two vowel rows within a speaker.

We will make the pieces line up for one speaker-level duration target: the parameter and its null value, the estimator, its standard error, and the reference distribution. Once they are aligned, we can say exactly what the standardized statistic measures before turning to its tail probability on the next page.

## A within-speaker target

For each Hillenbrand adult woman, let

$$
D_s=Y_{s,/I/}-Y_{s,/i/}
$$

be the duration of /I/ in *hid* minus /i/ in *heed*. Pairing first makes the speaker the observation and removes stable speaker-level duration differences from the contrast.

```{r}
#| label: hillenbrand-null-data
library(ggplot2)

vowels <- read.csv(
  "data/hillenbrand/vowels-complete.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
long <- subset(vowels, speaker_type == "woman" & vowel %in% c("I", "i"),
               select = c(speaker_id, vowel, duration_ms))
paired <- reshape(long, idvar = "speaker_id", timevar = "vowel", direction = "wide")
names(paired)[names(paired) == "duration_ms.I"] <- "hid_ms"
names(paired)[names(paired) == "duration_ms.i"] <- "heed_ms"
paired$difference_ms <- paired$hid_ms - paired$heed_ms

n <- nrow(paired)
d_bar <- mean(paired$difference_ms)
s_d <- sd(paired$difference_ms)
se_d <- s_d / sqrt(n)

stopifnot(n == 48L, !anyNA(paired$difference_ms))
data.frame(speakers = n, mean_difference_ms = d_bar,
           sd_difference_ms = s_d, se_ms = se_d)
```

## The null and statistic

The target is the mean within-speaker difference $\mu_D$. The point null is

$$
H_0:\mu_D=0,
$$

and the two-sided alternative is

$$
H_1:\mu_D\neq0.
$$

The standardized statistic is

$$
T(\mathbf D)
=\frac{\overline D-0}{s_D/\sqrt n}.
$$

Before observation, $T(\mathbf D)$ is random. After observing $\mathbf D=\mathbf d$, its value is $t_{\mathrm{obs}}=T(\mathbf d)$. Under $H_0$ and the normal independent-difference assumptions derived on the [one-sample t page](one-sample-t-inference.qmd#from-a-standardized-mean-to-a-t-reference),

$$
T(\mathbf D)\mid H_0\sim t_{n-1}.
$$

The two-sided p value is the null-reference probability of a statistic at least as far from zero as the observed value:

$$
p_{\mathrm{two\ sided}}
=
\mathbb{P}_{H_0}
\left(
|T(\mathbf D)|\geq |t_{\mathrm{obs}}|
\right)
=2F_{t_{n-1}}(-|t_{\mathrm{obs}}|).
$$

```{r}
#| label: compute-hillenbrand-null-statistic
t_observed <- d_bar / se_d
degrees_of_freedom <- n - 1L
two_sided_p <- 2 * pt(-abs(t_observed), df = degrees_of_freedom)

data.frame(t = t_observed, df = degrees_of_freedom, p_value = two_sided_p)
```

The observed mean difference is `r sprintf("%.3f", d_bar)` ms and the standardized discrepancy is $t=$ `r sprintf("%.3f", t_observed)`.

In the code, `t_observed <- d_bar / se_d` evaluates $T(\mathbf d)$ and `2 * pt(-abs(t_observed), df = degrees_of_freedom)` evaluates the two symmetric tail areas under the $t_{n-1}$ reference distribution.

```{r}
#| label: plot-hillenbrand-null-differences
#| fig-cap: "Within-speaker duration differences. The line is the null value and the red point is the observed mean."
ggplot(paired, aes(1, difference_ms)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey65", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(color = "grey35", alpha = 0.75, width = 0.08, height = 0, # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
              seed = 20261018) +
  geom_point(data = data.frame(x = 1, y = d_bar), aes(x, y),
             inherit.aes = FALSE, color = "#8B1A1A", size = 2.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Within-speaker /I/ - /i/ duration (ms)") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

A small tail probability measures incompatibility with this null model. It is not the probability that $H_0$ is true, and it does not replace the effect estimate or its units.

## Recap and forward link

1. $T(\mathbf D)$ is a random statistic under the null model; $t_{\mathrm{obs}}$ is its observed value.
2. The p value is a probability over hypothetical statistics under $H_0$, not a probability assigned to $H_0$. <!-- dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation -->
3. Pairing, independence across speakers, and the reference-distribution assumptions license the calculation.

The [one-sample t page](one-sample-t-inference.qmd#from-a-standardized-mean-to-a-t-reference) now derives that reference distribution and the corresponding interval.

## Check your understanding

1. Why is the null value expressed in milliseconds?
2. Which quantity standardizes the observed discrepancy?
3. Why must the vowel rows be paired before calculating the statistic?
4. What does the tail probability condition on?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The parameter is a mean within-speaker duration difference, so zero and any alternative value have millisecond units. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The standard error $s_D/\sqrt n$ standardizes the observed mean difference from the null value. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Pairing forms one within-speaker contrast and removes stable between-speaker duration differences from the statistic. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. The $t$-test tail probability conditions on the point null and its reference model, including independent speaker differences and the $t$ reference assumptions. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
